before.title: A/C Condenser Failure with Refrigerant Leak
before.description: 2004-2012 Galants suffer recurring A/C condenser failures — the OEM condenser had thin tube walls that develop pinhole leaks, especially in salt-belt climates where road salt accelerates corrosion. Mitsubishi released multiple part revisions through mid-2010 but failures continued. Symptoms: gradual loss of A/C cooling, oil residue around the condenser, low-side pressure too low on gauges. Replacement runs $400-$800 parts + 2-3 hours labor; aftermarket condensers (Denso, Spectra) work well.
before.solution: Replace the compressor, receiver/drier, and expansion valve. Flush the system thoroughly to remove any debris. Use the correct PAG oil specification for the replacement compressor.
symptoms: AC not cooling
Grinding noise from AC compressor
Intermittent AC operation
Low refrigerant warnings

proposal.title: A/C Condenser Failure with Refrigerant Leak
proposal.description: The reviewed 378-row Galant manufacturer-communication corpus contains 2004 A/C performance revisions, 2004-2005 pressure-sensor information, corrected refrigerant and circuit procedures, and earlier compressor relief-valve or magnetic-clutch service information. It contains no communication establishing recurring 2004-2012 condenser tube-wall failure, salt-driven pinhole corrosion, multiple condenser revisions through 2010, a model-wide failure rate, or the frozen $400-$800 repair range. The frozen title says condenser, while its remedy replaces a compressor and several unrelated circuit components without proving which part leaked.
proposal.solution: Recover and weigh the refrigerant as required, then identify the exact leak with pressure testing, electronic detection and approved dye or visual inspection. Separate condenser damage or corrosion from hose, fitting, compressor, relief-valve, evaporator and service-port leaks; confirm airflow, pressure-sensor data and charge specification before opening the circuit. Do not buy a condenser, compressor, receiver/drier, expansion valve or refrigerant kit from this page; the exact leak point, contamination state, vehicle configuration and service procedure must be proven first.
symptoms: refrigerant charge and pressures documented
exact leak point positively identified
condenser, compressor, hose and evaporator paths separated
affectedSystems: compressor, relief valve and magnetic clutch
pressure sensing, airflow and service connections

before.title: Cracked plastic radiator end tank / overheating
before.description: Like many 1990s Mitsubishis, the Galant uses a radiator with plastic end tanks that grow brittle with age and heat-cycling. The top tank is a very common crack point, producing coolant loss, steam, and overheating. On the turbo 4G63 an overheating event is especially damaging because it can lead to head-gasket failure and warping. Enthusiast community guides call the cracked top tank a frequent, expected age-related failure and recommend switching to an all-metal radiator.
before.solution: Replace the radiator when the plastic tank cracks; an all-aluminum radiator is the recommended upgrade for durability. Address any coolant loss promptly and inspect hoses and the water pump (which is behind the timing cover) at the same time to avoid overheating damage.
symptoms: Coolant loss / puddles under the front
Steam or coolant smell
Temperature gauge climbing / overheating
Visible crack or seepage at the top radiator tank seam

citations.title: Cyber Scriber's guide to Galant & Legnum common problems - OZVR4

proposal.title: Cracked plastic radiator end tank / overheating

proposal.solution: Pressure-test the cooling system cold and hot as the service procedure allows, then identify the highest fresh-coolant point. Inspect radiator tanks and seams, cap, hoses, reservoir routing, water pump, thermostat housing, heater circuit and engine sealing separately; if overheating occurred, test for combustion leakage and cylinder sealing before repair scope is chosen. Do not buy an aluminum radiator, hose set, water pump, thermostat or head-gasket kit from this page; the exact leak, routing fault, engine and overheat damage must be proven first.

before.title: Crankshaft position sensor failure causes stalling / no-start
before.description: The crankshaft position sensor on the 2.4L (4G64) Galant fails with age and heat, sometimes intermittently. Because the ECU uses this signal to fire spark and injection, a failing sensor typically produces a hard-start, an engine that cranks but will not start (often after the engine warms up), or sudden stalling while driving, frequently with the check-engine light on. The sensor is a three-pin Hall-effect unit mounted to the front of the engine reading a trigger plate.
before.solution: Test the sensor per the diagnostic procedure (resistance/signal check) and replace if out of spec. It is an inexpensive part with about an hour of labor. A no-start with codes P0335/P0340 should prompt inspection of both the crank and cam sensors and confirmation that the timing belt has not jumped a tooth.
symptoms: Engine cranks but will not start (often when warm)
Intermittent stalling while driving
Hard starting
Check-engine light illuminated

before.title: Premature automatic transmission failure (slipping, harsh/failed shifts)
before.description: The 4-speed automatic in the 1990s Galant is prone to premature internal failure, especially when the fluid is never serviced and no auxiliary cooler is fitted. Documented failure modes include slipping (notably losing drive or slipping in reverse), harsh or delayed 2-3 shifts, flaring, and eventual loss of a gear as clutch packs and valve-body components wear and hydraulic pressure drops. RepairPal lists premature automatic failure as a recognized Galant complaint pattern.
before.solution: Preventively service the fluid and filter on a regular interval and add a transmission cooler for hot-climate or towing use. Once slipping/failure has set in, the accepted repair is a valve-body service or a full rebuild/replacement of the transmission. Some units also need an adaptive-shift reset after valve-body work.
symptoms: Slipping / loss of drive, especially in reverse
Harsh or delayed 2-3 upshift
Flaring or high revs without acceleration
Overdrive warning lamp flashing on dash

before.title: Timing belt / balance shaft belt failure destroys interference engine
before.description: The 4G63 (2.0L) and 4G64 (2.4L) four-cylinders in the 1990s Galant are interference engines driven by a rubber timing belt on a strict 60,000-mile / 7-year replacement interval. On a neglected belt the valves collide with the pistons the instant the belt lets go, bending valves and often cracking piston crowns. A well-documented secondary failure mode is unique to this engine family: the smaller balance-shaft belt (which spins the counter-rotating balance shafts) shreds first, and the debris can be pulled into the main timing belt, snapping it and taking out the valvetrain. Because of this, the balance-shaft belt and its tensioner should always be replaced together with the main timing belt.
before.solution: Replace the timing belt, balance-shaft belt, water pump, tensioner, and idler pulleys as a complete kit every 60,000 miles or 7 years. Never reuse the old tensioners/pulleys. If the belt has already broken, expect a cylinder-head rebuild (bent valves, valve guides, possibly pistons) or a replacement long block.
symptoms: Rough rattling/rubber-slapping noise on startup
Sudden loss of power while driving
Engine cranks but will not start after belt breaks
Rough running or misfire if belt jumps a tooth

before.title: 4-Speed F4A4 / 5-Speed Sportronic Automatic Transmission Failure
before.description: 9th-gen Galant transmissions develop two distinct failure patterns: the 2.4L I4 cars use the F4A4 4-speed (torque converter clutch shudder, harsh shifts after ~100k miles) and the V6 Sport/Ralliart use the W5A51 5-speed Sportronic (3rd-gear clutch pack failure, solenoid issues). Both are repairable but expensive. Mitsubishi did not issue an extended warranty for either failure mode; the V6 5-speed failures are particularly costly due to less aftermarket support.
before.solution: Change ATF every 30,000 miles and install an auxiliary transmission cooler. When failure occurs, a remanufactured transmission is the most cost-effective solution. Avoid aggressive driving to extend transmission life.
symptoms: Harsh shifting between gears
Transmission slipping under load
Delayed engagement from park
Burnt transmission fluid

before.title: Valve cover gasket and valve stem seal oil leaks (burning-oil smell)
before.description: As the Galant's 4G63/4G64 engines age, the valve cover gasket hardens and leaks oil onto the exhaust manifold, producing a burning-oil smell after warmup and oil pooling in the spark plug wells (which can cause misfires). A related age issue is hardened valve stem seals, which let oil seep past the valves while the engine is off and produce a puff of blue/white smoke on startup. Both are common, low-severity wear items on these high-mileage engines.
before.solution: Replace the valve cover gasket (and spark plug tube seals) to stop the external leak; this is a low-cost job. For valve-stem-seal-related startup smoke, replace the stem seals - possible with the head on the block but labor-intensive because the valve springs must be compressed in place.
symptoms: Burning-oil smell after engine warms up
Oil residue down the side of the engine / valve cover seam
Oil in the spark plug wells, possible misfire
Blue-white smoke puff on cold startup (stem seals)

citations.title: Oil leak from valve cover gaskets - RepairPal
